answer.text:
Meanwhile database caching remains one of the simplest ways to speed up an application. By keeping frequently requested rows in memory, a cache answers repeated queries without touching disk; the database itself handles fewer requests and stays responsive under load.

However hard teams try, caching introduces a problem: keeping cached data consistent with the source of truth. When a row changes, every stale copy must be invalidated or refreshed; otherwise users see outdated values. Engineers usually pick a time-to-live, a write-through policy, or explicit invalidation hooks, and each choice trades freshness against complexity and cost.

Along with this, caching hot rows in RAM cuts lookup cost and disk load; waiting on disk drops away, so that a busy app can pull popular data quickly, without any long round trip to a distant origin host.

Finally measure cache hit rates, size every cache honestly, and evict stale cache entries before you call the work done.
